listening.title: The University Seed Library
listening.focus: Main ideas, details and a corrected detail
listening.script: Mr Lee: Good morning, welcome to the university seed library. How can I help you? Maya: Good morning. I am a first-year biology student, and I heard I can borrow seeds here for free. Is that right? Mr Lee: Yes, that is right. The seed library lets students take home small packets of vegetable and flower seeds, grow them, and later return new seeds if the plants grow well. Maya: That sounds interesting. How do I join? Mr Lee: You just need to fill in a short form with your name, student number, and email. Then you can choose up to three packets each month. Maya: Only three? I thought I could take five. Mr Lee: The guide on the website says five, but we changed it this term to three, because demand is high. So three packets is the new limit. Maya: I understand. What kinds of seeds do you have now? Mr Lee: At the moment, we have tomatoes, carrots, beans, and sunflowers. Beans are the most popular because they grow quickly, even in small pots. Maya: I would like to try beans and sunflowers. Do I need anything else? Mr Lee: We also ask you to keep a simple growing diary. Just write the planting date, where you put the pot, and how often you water the plant. It helps you notice problems. Maya: Do I have to return seeds at the end? Mr Lee: If you can, yes. If your sunflowers produce seeds, bring some back in a clean, dry envelope with the plant name and date. But if the plant does not grow well, just tell us. There is no fine. Maya: That is good. Is there any training? I have never grown flowers before. Mr Lee: Yes, we have a short beginners workshop. It was planned for Thursday, but sorry, it moved to Friday at 2 p.m. in Room 3 of the library. It takes about one hour. Maya: Perfect, I can come on Friday. How long can I keep the seeds before planting? Mr Lee: Please plant them within four weeks, and keep the packets in a cool, dry place until then. Maya: Thank you very much. I will fill in the form now.

reading.title: The Campus Repair Workshop
reading.focus: Main ideas, details, claim versus example and simple inference
reading.passage: The Campus Repair Workshop opened last year in the basement of the Student Centre. It is a free service where students can bring small broken things and learn how to fix them with help from trained volunteers. The idea is simple: instead of throwing things away, students repair and reuse them. The workshop is open on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. Students do not need an appointment. They just bring the broken item and wait for a volunteer. The volunteers do not fix things alone. They show the student each step, so the student learns the skill. Common repairs include bicycles with flat tyres, jackets with broken zips, and phones with cracked screen covers. The workshop does not repair large electrical items, such as fridges, because they can be dangerous. All tools and basic materials are provided at the workshop, so students do not need to buy anything in advance. Last month, second-year student Lena brought in a desk lamp that stopped working. A volunteer helped her open the base, test the wire, and change the small switch inside. The repair took about forty minutes and cost only two dollars for the new switch. Lena said she was happy because she uses the lamp every evening for study. This story is one example of a normal repair at the workshop. It does not mean every repair is quick or cheap, but it shows how the process works. The organiser's report makes a clear claim: the main value of the workshop is learning, not saving money. In other words, students gain useful practical skills and confidence, and saving money is only a second benefit. The report also says the workshop helps the environment by reducing waste. Last term, volunteers recorded 310 repairs, and 210 items worked again after the visit. That means fewer things went into the bins. The service is open to all students from any subject. To use the workshop well, students should follow three rules. First, clean the item before bringing it. Second, bring any extra parts, such as buttons or batteries, if you have them. Third, stay for the whole repair and listen to the safety advice. The waiting time can be long on busy days, sometimes more than one hour, so many students bring study notes while they wait. The organisers hope more students will join as volunteers next term after a short training course.

writingPrompts.focus: Clear main ideas and direct comparison from table data
writingPrompts.prompt: This is original practice material. The table below shows the number of seed packets borrowed from the Greenfield University seed library from March to May 2026. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words in about 20 minutes. Table data: Vegetables - March 120, April 150, May 180; Flowers - March 80, April 95, May 110; Herbs - March 60, April 70, May 65. All figures are numbers of packets borrowed by students.

writingPrompts.focus: Clear opinion with direct evidence from familiar student life
writingPrompts.prompt: This is original practice material. Some students at Greenfield University keep a sleep-and-study diary for one month. They write down their bedtime, wake-up time, and study hours each day. Some people think this is a good way to improve study habits. Do you agree or disagree? Give reasons for your answer and include examples from your own experience or studies. Write in clear paragraphs with a simple introduction and conclusion. Write at least 250 words in about 40 minutes.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words in about 20 minutes. writingPrompts.focus: Simple explanation of advantages with clear main ideas

Greenfield University has opened a free campus repair workshop where students can learn to fix these things with help from staff. Some people think all universities should have this kind of workshop. Do you agree or disagree? Give reasons for your answer and include examples from your own life or studies. Write at least 250 words in about 40 minutes.

writingPrompts.task: Task 2 · Seed Libraries and Student Community
writingPrompts.focus: Balanced discussion with accurate simple explanations
writingPrompts.prompt: This is original practice material. Greenfield University has a seed library where students can borrow vegetable, flower and herb seeds for free, grow plants at home, and return new seeds later. Some people think this helps students learn about nature and community life. Others think the university should spend money on books and computers instead. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons and examples from your experience. Write at least 250 words in about 40 minutes.

speakingPrompts.focus: Familiar academic context and simple personal explanations
speakingPrompts.prompt: This is original practice material for Part 1, 4-5 minutes. Answer in short, clear sentences. 1. What time do you usually go to bed and get up? 2. Where do you like to study, at home or at the university? 3. Do you ever write down your study hours or sleep hours? Why or why not? 4. What helps you concentrate when you study?

speakingPrompts.focus: Familiar topics with direct personal evidence
speakingPrompts.prompt: This is original practice material for Part 1, 4-5 minutes. Answer in short, clear sentences. 1. Do you like growing plants or vegetables? Why or why not? 2. Is there a garden or green space near your home or university? 3. Have you ever borrowed books or seeds from a library? 4. Do you like to fix or reuse old things?

speakingPrompts.task: Part 2 · Cue card - A Record You Kept
speakingPrompts.focus: Clear description with simple sequence and reason
speakingPrompts.prompt: This is original practice material for Part 2. You have one minute to prepare and should speak for one to two minutes. Describe a diary or record you kept about your sleep, study, or daily life. You should say: what you recorded and for how long, when and where you did it, what you learned from the record, and explain why it was useful or not useful for you.

speakingPrompts.focus: Giving reasons and simple evaluation, not memorised facts
speakingPrompts.prompt: This is original practice material for Part 3, 4-5 minutes. Give reasons and explain your ideas. 1. Why do some university students sleep late and feel tired in class? 2. How can keeping a sleep-and-study diary help students understand their habits? 3. Do you think universities should teach students about sleep and health? Why? 4. Which is more important for good study results, longer study hours or better sleep? Why?

speakingPrompts.task: Part 3 · Repair, Reuse and Campus Life
speakingPrompts.focus: Reasons and evaluation of community ideas
speakingPrompts.prompt: This is original practice material for Part 3, 4-5 minutes. Give reasons and evaluate ideas. 1. Why do many students throw away things that could be repaired? 2. What are the advantages of a campus repair workshop for students and the community? 3. Are there any problems with running a free repair service at a university? 4. How can activities like a seed library or a repair workshop change student life in the future?
